entry.title: The 8 Ways to Make Money from Open Source (Ranked by How Long They'll Survive AI)
entry.content:
There are exactly eight ways people make money from open source. Some of them are about to get much harder. Some were never about the code to begin with — and those are the ones that will outlive the current shift.

Here is the full landscape, ranked by how well each model survives a world where any competent developer with an agent can rebuild your product in a weekend.

1. Selling support and operations

The Red Hat model. Nobody ever paid Red Hat for Linux — Linux was free. They paid for accountability: someone to call, someone to escalate to, someone the auditors can put on a slide.

Agents can generate code. They cannot be on the hook at 3am when your deployment eats itself. Survives AI untouched.

2. Hosting and managed services

Uptime is a track record, not a feature. An agent can generate a Supabase clone in a weekend. It cannot generate five years of 99.99% uptime history, a SOC2 report, or a security team that has handled a real breach.

Survives AI — arguably gets stronger.

3. Sponsorships

Sponsors fund humans and track records, not repos. Nobody sponsors a codebase. The donation button on a maintainer profile converts because of years of visible, verifiable work.

Survives AI untouched.

4. Selling the whole product to enterprises (governance, not features)

The quiet winner. SSO, audit logs, RBAC — companies pay for these not because the code is hard, but because their compliance regime requires someone accountable to provide them. “My agent built our own SSO” does not survive a SOC2 audit.

Survives AI — the compliance surface is the product.

5. Grants and foundations

NLnet, Sovereign Tech Fund, Open Collective fiscal hosting. Grant bodies fund public goods and stewardship — a category agents cannot fabricate.

Survives AI.

6. Paid work and bounties

Algora-style issue bounties. Works, but watch the new failure mode: agent-generated low-effort bounty claims flooding your queue. Viable with screening.

Survives AI with friction.

7. Open core with feature gates

The paid tier exists because the features took months to build. But a clone doesn’t care about your months. Feature-gating weakens badly when generation is free — gate on operations and governance instead, or lose the tier.

Weakened by AI.

8. Dual licensing and license fees

The “pay or we get copied” threat only worked when copying was expensive. It isn’t anymore. Selling legal certainty still works for compliance-driven corporates — but as a threat, it’s hollow.

Most weakened by AI.

The pattern

Every model that survives is selling something that is not the code: accountability, uptime, a track record, a compliance surface, stewardship. Every model that dies is selling the code itself.

That is not a coincidence. It is the whole thesis of this blog: code is free now. Someone who will still be fixing it in three years is not — and that asymmetry is the business model.

Before you pick a model, check how projects already running it score on maintenance health over at the open source scorecards. The winners of the AI era will be the projects that are still alive in three years.

entry.title: Why Nobody Will Pay for Code Anymore
entry.content:
A few weeks ago I watched an agent rebuild a closed-source SaaS tool as an open-source clone. Over a weekend. Not because anyone asked it to — someone on the internet complained about the pricing, an agent session spun up, and by Monday there was a working alternative with a README, CI, and a MIT license.

I have been writing software for 25+ years. I have sold software. And that weekend broke something in my head that I don’t think gets repaired.

Here is the thing: we priced software on scarcity that no longer exists. Code was expensive because writing it took senior humans a long time. That input cost is collapsing, and with it the output price. When any competent developer with an agent can rebuild your product in a weekend, “buy my code” stops being a pitch. It becomes a museum exhibit.

What dies

Feature-gated open core is the first casualty. The paid tier exists because the features took months to build — but a clone doesn’t care about your months. Dual licensing weakens next: the “pay or we get copied” threat only worked when copying was expensive. And source-available licenses built to stop cloud providers wrapping your repo? The cloud provider doesn’t need your repo anymore. It can rebuild you from screenshots.

None of this is a licensing problem. The license was never the moat — it was a fence painted around a moat that used to be there.

What hardens

Look at what people actually paid for in the last decade of open source, and notice it was almost never the code.

Sponsorships. Red Hat didn’t get to $1B selling Linux — you can download Linux for free, and always could. They sold accountability: someone to call, someone to escalate to, someone your auditors can put on a slide. Sponsors fund maintainers, not repos. Nobody sponsors a codebase.

Hosting. Uptime is a track record, not a feature. Your agent can generate a Supabase clone in a weekend — it cannot generate five years of 99.99% uptime history, a SOC2 report, or a security team that has actually handled a breach at 3am.

And the quiet one: maintenance itself. Generation is a one-shot event. Survival is a grind measured in years. Every abandoned project now gets ten eager clones within a week — and none of those clones will be patched either, because the people who generated them were solving for “exists”, not “stays alive”.

The uncomfortable summary

Code is free. Someone who will still be fixing it in three years is not.

That asymmetry is the entire business model now. If you maintain open source, your money is not in the code — it is in being the person who is still there. Verifiable maintenance history, the thing my scorecards project tries to measure, is the closest thing left to a moat you can actually build.

So if you are sitting on an open source project wondering how to monetize it: stop asking what feature you can charge for. Ask who would miss you if you stopped showing up. That answer is your product.

The clone has your code. It will never have your Tuesday.
